extra.message: The 'linkPartyRecord' service (invoking PartyServices.linkParty, lines 1950-2185 of PartyServices.java) is declared with only auth="true" and no <permission-service> element, unlike every sibling party-mutation service in this file (createPartyAttribute/updatePartyAttribute/setPartyStatus/updatePerson/updatePartyGroup all require partyBasePermissionCheck/partyGroupPermissionCheck/partyStatusPermissionCheck). It is exposed at applications/party/webapp/partymgr/WEB-INF/controller.xml lines 112-118 as request-map 'setPartyLink', also guarded by auth="true" only. Inside linkParty(), 'partyId' and 'partyIdTo' are taken directly from the request with no ownership/permission check, and the method reassigns PartyContactMech, PartyNote, InventoryItem.ownerPartyId, Subscription, UserLogin.partyId, PartyRole, OrderRole, InvoiceRole, FinAccountRole, ProductStoreRole, ContentRole from partyId to partyIdTo, then disables partyId. Any authenticated user able to reach the Party Manager webapp can call setPartyLink?partyId=<victim>&partyIdTo=<attacker-party> to hijack another party's login, inventory ownership, financial-account roles and order/invoice roles, and disable the victim party.

extra.message: openSourceFile() builds a shell command template (widget.dev.cmd.openSourceFile) expanded with request-derived 'sourceLocation' (request.getParameter, line 402) and passes the result to Runtime.getRuntime().exec(new String[]{cmd}). The path is restricted via SecurityUtil.checkOfbizFileAllowList() (line 420) and the feature is gated behind the non-default widget.dev.namedBorder=SOURCE setting, which limits exploitability, but it remains unsafe use of Runtime.exec with HTTP-request-influenced data feeding directly into process execution.

validatePin() logs both the submitted PIN and the real FinAccount.finAccountCode (the gift-certificate/financial-account PIN) in plaintext at INFO level: Debug.logInfo("GC Pin Validation: [Sent: " + pinNumber + "] [Actual: " + dbPin + "]", MODULE). INFO is enabled by default, so any user/process with log read access can recover every gift-card PIN that has ever been validated, including guessed/failed values paired with the real secret.

extra.message: putFile() logs the FTP password in plaintext at INFO level: Debug.logInfo("[putFile] logging in: username=" + username + ", password=" + password, MODULE). On login failure the same plaintext password is also embedded into the user-facing error message via UtilProperties.getMessage(RESOURCE, "CommonFtpLoginFailure", UtilMisc.toMap("username", username, "password", password), locale) (CommonUiLabels.xml: 'Login failed (${username}, ${password})'), returned to the service caller through ServiceUtil.returnError. This exposes the FTP credential both in logs and in the service response.

extra.message: setContentDisposition() builds the Content-Disposition header with response.setHeader("Content-Disposition", String.format("%s; filename=\"%s\"", dispositionType, filename)) with no escaping of embedded quote or control characters in 'filename'. It is called from applications/content/.../DataEvents.java:231 with dataResource.getString("dataResourceName"), a field an authenticated user can set when creating/uploading a DataResource. An embedded '"' lets the value break out of the filename="..." token and append extra Content-Disposition parameters.

extra.message: sendMailFromUrl() takes 'bodyUrl' directly as a required service IN-parameter (services_email.xml lines 96-102, no auth="true"/export restriction and no host allow-list), builds a URI/URL from it (lines 443-445) and performs a server-side HTTP POST via 'new HttpClient(url, bodyUrlParameters)' / 'httpClient.post()' with no scheme or host validation — unlike the hardened URL_RESOURCE fetch path in DataResourceWorker.java which enforces an http/https + host allow-list and blocks redirects. Any caller able to invoke this service (directly via the service engine, or any export mechanism that lists it) can make the server issue arbitrary outbound HTTP requests, including to internal-only hosts.

The incoming SOAP request body is parsed with 'OMXMLBuilderFactory.createSOAPModelBuilder(request.getInputStream(), "UTF-8")' / 'builder.getDocumentElement()' with no XMLInputFactory hardening (no IS_SUPPORTING_EXTERNAL_ENTITIES=false / SUPPORT_DTD=false), unlike every other XML entry point in this same class (the outgoing response builders at lines 243-245 and 299-301 are correctly hardened). A remote caller's SOAP envelope is fed straight into this unhardened parser, a classic XXE sink. Reachability requires the 'soap' handler and request-map (currently commented out by default in handlers-controller.xml and webtools controller.xml, citing OFBIZ-12212) to be re-enabled by an administrator.

extra.message: resolveClass() validates deserialized class names with 'allowlistPattern.matcher(className).find()' against patterns like "java\\.lang\\.String" (lines 40-72) that are neither anchored (no ^/$) nor matched with .matches(). Because .find() only requires the pattern to appear as a substring anywhere in the class name, a class whose fully-qualified name merely contains an allowed token (e.g. 'evil.java.lang.String.Gadget') would incorrectly pass the allowlist check, weakening this deserialization gate used throughout the framework (UtilObject, JdbcValueHandler, EntityCrypto, RequestHandler). No concrete gadget class with such a name was found on the current classpath, so this is a design/implementation weakness rather than a demonstrated live exploit.
